words.definition: The symmetric, bell-shaped distribution described by its mean and standard deviation.
words.example: In a normal distribution, about 68% of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean.

words.definition: A distribution for the waiting time between events that occur at a constant average rate.
words.example: The time until the next bus can be modelled with an exponential distribution.

words.definition: How many standard deviations a value is from the mean.
words.example: A score of 85 with mean 70 and SD 10 has a z-score of 1.5.

words.definition: The whole group you want to learn about.
words.example: All first-year students at the university form the population.

words.definition: A subset of the population that is actually measured.
words.example: We surveyed a sample of 200 students.

words.definition: A sample where every member of the population has a known, fair chance of being chosen.
words.example: A random sample avoids picking only your friends.

words.definition: Error caused when the sample does not represent the population.
words.example: Surveying only the library creates sampling bias.

words.definition: A number that describes a population, such as the true mean.
words.example: The average height of all students is a parameter.

words.definition: A number calculated from a sample.
words.example: The sample mean is a statistic.

words.definition: A rule for estimating a parameter from sample data.
words.example: The sample mean is an estimator of the population mean.

words.definition: As the sample grows, the sample average gets closer to the expected value.
words.example: By the law of large numbers, many die rolls average close to 3.5.

words.definition: For large samples, the sample mean is approximately normally distributed, whatever the population's shape (if its variance is finite).
words.example: The central limit theorem is why confidence intervals often use the normal curve.

words.definition: A range of values, built from a sample, that is likely to contain the true parameter.
words.example: The 95% confidence interval for the mean was 68 to 72.

words.definition: A procedure that uses sample data to decide whether evidence supports rejecting a claim about a population.
words.example: A hypothesis test checked whether the new app improves scores.

words.definition: The default claim of no effect or no difference, written H0.
words.example: The null hypothesis says the new method makes no difference.

words.definition: The claim you look for evidence of, written H1 or Ha.
words.example: The alternative hypothesis says the new method raises scores.

words.definition: The probability of getting results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true.
words.example: A p-value of 0.01 is strong evidence against the null hypothesis.

words.definition: The threshold α for rejecting the null hypothesis, often 0.05.
words.example: With a significance level of 0.05, p = 0.03 leads to rejecting H0.

words.definition: Rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true; a false positive.
words.example: Convicting an innocent person is like a type I error.

words.definition: Failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false; a false negative.
words.example: Missing a real disease in a test is a type II error.

words.definition: A measure from -1 to 1 of how strongly two variables move together in a straight-line pattern.
words.example: Study time and exam score showed a correlation of 0.6.

words.definition: A measure of how two variables change together; its sign shows the direction.
words.example: Positive covariance means both tend to rise together.

words.definition: Fitting a straight line that predicts one variable from another.
words.example: Linear regression predicted exam scores from study hours.

subjects.name: Software Engineering
subjects.description: Planning, building, testing and maintaining software in teams.

words.definition: Applying systematic, disciplined methods to building and maintaining software.
words.example: Software engineering is more than writing code; it includes planning and testing.

words.definition: The stages software goes through: requirements, design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
words.example: Testing is one phase of the software development life cycle.

words.definition: Anyone with an interest in a project, such as users, clients or managers.
words.example: Interview every stakeholder before writing requirements.

words.definition: A statement of what the system must do or a quality it must have.
words.example: "Users can reset their password" is a requirement.

words.definition: A requirement describing a specific behaviour or function.
words.example: "The app shows a quiz of 10 words" is a functional requirement.

words.definition: A requirement about qualities such as speed, security or usability.
words.example: "Pages load in under 2 seconds" is a non-functional requirement.

words.definition: A detailed, precise description of what a system must do.
words.example: The specification lists every screen in the app.

words.definition: A description of how a user interacts with the system to reach a goal.
words.example: "Student takes a quiz" is a use case.

words.definition: A short requirement written from the user's view: As a ..., I want ..., so that ....
words.example: "As a student, I want to review missed words so that I can remember them" is a user story.

words.definition: Conditions a feature must meet to count as done.
words.example: The acceptance criteria say the quiz must show the correct answer after each question.

words.definition: A process where each phase finishes completely before the next one starts.
words.example: The waterfall model suits projects with fixed requirements.

words.definition: Describes development in short cycles, delivering working software often and adapting to change.
words.example: Our team works in an agile way with two-week sprints.

words.definition: An agile framework with sprints, a product backlog and set team roles.
words.example: In Scrum, the team meets daily for a stand-up.

words.definition: A fixed time period, often 1 to 4 weeks, in which a team delivers a set of work.
words.example: This sprint we will finish the quiz screen.

words.definition: An ordered list of all work wanted for a product.
words.example: New feature ideas go into the product backlog.

words.definition: A short daily meeting where each member shares progress and blockers.
words.example: In the stand-up meeting she said she was blocked by a bug.

words.definition: A method that visualises work on a board with columns such as To Do, Doing, Done.
words.example: Our Kanban board shows three tasks in progress.

words.definition: One repeated cycle of development that produces an improved version.
words.example: Each iteration added one game mode.

words.definition: An early, simple version of a system built to test ideas.
words.example: We showed users a paper prototype of the main screen.

words.definition: The simplest version of a product that still delivers value to users (MVP).
words.example: Our minimum viable product only has the multiple-choice game.

words.definition: The high-level structure of a system: its main parts and how they communicate.
words.example: Our software architecture splits the C++ core from the web front end.

words.definition: A self-contained part of a program with a clear job.
words.example: The quiz module doesn't know how words are loaded.

words.definition: How much one module depends on another; the lower, the better.
words.example: Passing data through function parameters keeps coupling low.

words.definition: How closely the parts of one module belong together; the higher, the better.
words.example: A class that only handles saving files has high cohesion.

words.definition: Unified Modeling Language: standard diagrams for designing software.
words.example: We drew UML diagrams for the classes and use cases.

words.definition: A UML diagram showing messages between objects over time.
words.example: The sequence diagram shows the login steps.

words.definition: A system that records changes to files over time so you can review and undo them.
words.example: Git is the most popular version control system.

words.definition: A storage location for a project's files and their full change history.
words.example: Clone the repository to get the code.

words.definition: A saved snapshot of changes in version control, with a message.
words.example: Each commit should describe one change.

words.definition: An independent line of development in a repository.
words.example: Create a branch for the new game mode.

words.definition: To combine changes from one branch into another.
words.example: Merge the feature branch into main after review.

words.definition: When two branches change the same lines and Git cannot combine them automatically.
words.example: We fixed the merge conflict in main.cpp by hand.

words.definition: A request to review and merge changes from one branch into another.
words.example: Open a pull request so a teammate can check your code.

words.definition: Other developers reading your code to find problems before it is merged.
words.example: Code review caught a memory leak.

words.definition: Agreed rules for formatting and writing code in a team.
words.example: Our coding standard uses camelCase for variables.

words.definition: Improving the structure of code without changing what it does.
words.example: Refactoring split the 300-line function into five small ones.

words.definition: The future cost of choosing a quick solution now instead of a better one.
words.example: Copy-pasted code adds technical debt.

words.definition: Running software to find defects and check it meets requirements.
words.example: Software testing found three bugs before release.

words.definition: A set of inputs, steps and expected results for checking one behaviour.
words.example: One test case checks the quiz with zero words.

words.definition: A test that checks one small piece of code, such as a function, on its own.
words.example: A unit test checks that loadSubjects reports missing words.

words.definition: A test that checks that several modules work together correctly.
words.example: An integration test loads real JSON and starts a quiz.

words.definition: A test of the complete, integrated system against its requirements.
words.example: The system test ran the whole app in a browser.

words.definition: A test, often with users or clients, to decide if the system is ready to accept.
words.example: Our teacher ran the acceptance test.

words.definition: Re-running tests to make sure new changes didn't break old features.
words.example: Regression tests caught that the new menu broke the quiz.

words.definition: Testing based on inputs and outputs without looking at the code.
words.example: Black-box testing checks the app as a user would.

words.definition: Testing designed using knowledge of the code's internal structure.
words.example: White-box testing makes sure every branch of the if runs.

words.definition: The share of the code that the tests actually run.
words.example: Our test coverage is 80% of lines.

words.definition: A fault in software that makes it behave incorrectly.
words.example: A bug made the score negative.

words.definition: Finding the cause of a bug and fixing it.
words.example: Debugging took longer than writing the feature.

words.definition: Checking that the software is built correctly, matching its specification.
words.example: Verification asks: are we building the product right?

words.definition: Checking that the software meets the user's real needs.
words.example: Validation asks: are we building the right product?

words.definition: Automatically building and testing code every time changes are pushed.
words.example: Continuous integration ran all tests on every pull request.

words.definition: Releasing software so users can use it.
words.example: Deployment put the new version on the website.

words.definition: A version of the software made available to users.
words.example: Release 1.0 includes three game modes.

words.definition: Fixing, updating and improving software after release.
words.example: Most of a system's cost is maintenance.

words.definition: Written material explaining how software works or how to use it.
words.example: The README is the project's main documentation.

words.definition: Predicting how much time or effort a task will take.
words.example: Our estimation was two days, but it took four.

subjects.name: Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing
subjects.description: How models learn from data, and how computers work with human language.

words.definition: Building systems that learn patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules.
words.example: Machine learning predicts which words a student will forget.

words.definition: The learned function that maps inputs to predictions.
words.example: The model takes an email and outputs spam or not spam.

words.definition: The process of adjusting a model's parameters so it fits the data.
words.example: Training took 20 minutes on a laptop.

words.definition: A collection of examples used to train or test a model.
words.example: The dataset has 10,000 labelled reviews.

words.definition: A measurable input property used by a model.
words.example: Word count is a feature of each review.

words.definition: The correct answer attached to a training example.
words.example: Each review has a label: positive or negative.

words.definition: Learning from examples that come with correct labels.
words.example: Predicting house prices from labelled sales is supervised learning.

words.definition: Finding structure in data that has no labels.
words.example: Grouping customers by behaviour is unsupervised learning.

words.definition: Learning by trial and error, guided by rewards and penalties.
words.example: A game-playing agent improves through reinforcement learning.

words.definition: Predicting which category an input belongs to.
words.example: Spam detection is a classification task.

words.definition: Predicting a continuous number.
words.example: Predicting tomorrow's temperature is regression.

words.definition: Grouping similar data points without labels.
words.example: Clustering grouped the words into topics.

words.definition: The part of the data the model learns from.
words.example: We used 80% of the data as the training set.

words.definition: Data held out to tune hyperparameters and choose between models.
words.example: The validation set picked the best learning rate.

words.definition: Data kept apart until the end to measure final performance.
words.example: Never train on the test set.

words.definition: When a model learns the training data too closely, including noise, and fails on new data.
words.example: 99% training accuracy but 60% test accuracy suggests overfitting.

words.definition: When a model is too simple to capture the pattern in the data.
words.example: A straight line fitting curved data is underfitting.

words.definition: How well a model performs on new, unseen data.
words.example: Good generalization is the real goal of training.

words.definition: Techniques that discourage overly complex models to reduce overfitting.
words.example: Adding an L2 penalty is a form of regularization.

words.definition: A function measuring how wrong the model's predictions are.
words.example: Mean squared error is a common loss function for regression.

words.definition: An optimisation method that repeatedly steps parameters in the direction that reduces the loss.
words.example: Gradient descent slowly lowered the loss over 50 epochs.

words.definition: The size of each step in gradient descent.
words.example: A learning rate that is too high makes training unstable.

words.definition: One complete pass through the training data.
words.example: The model trained for 10 epochs.

words.definition: A small group of examples processed together in one training step.
words.example: We used a batch of 32 sentences.

words.definition: A value the model learns during training, such as a weight.
words.example: The network has one million parameters.

words.definition: A setting chosen before training rather than learned, such as the learning rate.
words.example: The number of layers is a hyperparameter.

words.definition: A model built from layers of connected units that each compute a weighted sum and an activation.
words.example: A neural network recognised handwritten digits.

words.definition: One unit in a neural network that combines inputs with weights and applies an activation function.
words.example: Each neuron outputs a single number.

words.definition: A group of neurons that process data at the same stage.
words.example: The hidden layer has 128 neurons.

words.definition: A non-linear function applied to a neuron's output, such as ReLU or sigmoid.
words.example: ReLU is the most common activation function.

words.definition: The algorithm that computes how much each weight contributed to the loss, using the chain rule.
words.example: Backpropagation gives the gradients that gradient descent needs.

words.definition: Machine learning with neural networks that have many layers.
words.example: Speech recognition improved greatly with deep learning.

words.definition: A model that predicts by asking a sequence of yes/no questions about features.
words.example: The decision tree first asks whether the review contains "terrible".

words.definition: A method that predicts using the k most similar training examples.
words.example: With k = 3, k-nearest neighbours takes a vote among the 3 closest points.

words.definition: A clustering algorithm that assigns points to k groups around repeatedly updated centres.
words.example: k-means split the students into 3 study groups.

words.definition: The share of predictions that are correct.
words.example: 90 correct out of 100 gives 90% accuracy.

words.definition: Of the items predicted positive, the share that really are positive.
words.example: High precision means few false alarms.

words.definition: Of the items that really are positive, the share the model found.
words.example: High recall means few positives are missed.

words.definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
words.example: Precision 0.8 and recall 0.6 give an F1 score of about 0.69.

words.definition: A table counting true and false positives and negatives.
words.example: The confusion matrix showed many cats labelled as dogs.

words.definition: Evaluating a model by training and testing on several different splits of the data.
words.example: 5-fold cross-validation gave a more reliable score.

words.definition: The field of making computers understand and produce human language (NLP).
words.example: Translation apps rely on natural language processing.

words.definition: A large collection of texts used for language study or training.
words.example: The model was trained on a corpus of news articles.

words.definition: A unit of text, such as a word, part of a word or punctuation mark, that a model processes.
words.example: "I love NLP!" can be split into 4 tokens.

words.definition: Splitting text into tokens.
words.example: Tokenization is the first step of most NLP pipelines.

words.definition: A very common word, such as "the" or "is", often removed before analysis.
words.example: Removing stop words shrinks the vocabulary.

words.definition: Cutting words down to a rough root form by chopping endings.
words.example: Stemming turns "studies" into "studi".

words.definition: Reducing words to their dictionary form using vocabulary and grammar.
words.example: Lemmatization turns "studies" into "study" and "better" into "good".

words.definition: The set of all distinct tokens a model knows.
words.example: Our vocabulary has 30,000 words.

words.definition: Representing text by word counts, ignoring word order.
words.example: In a bag of words, "dog bites man" equals "man bites dog".

words.definition: A word weight that is high when the word is frequent in one document but rare across others.
words.example: TF-IDF gives "pointer" a high score in a C++ article.

words.definition: A sequence of n consecutive tokens.
words.example: "machine learning" is a 2-gram (bigram).

words.definition: A vector of numbers representing a word so that similar words have similar vectors.
words.example: Word embeddings place "king" close to "queen".

words.definition: A model that assigns probabilities to sequences of words, often by predicting the next token.
words.example: A language model suggests the next word as you type.

words.definition: A neural network architecture built on attention, used by most modern language models.
words.example: The transformer architecture appeared in 2017.

words.definition: A mechanism that lets a model weigh how relevant each token is to every other token.
words.example: Attention links "it" to "the cat" in a sentence.

words.definition: Detecting whether text expresses a positive, negative or neutral opinion.
words.example: Sentiment analysis rated the app review as positive.

words.definition: Labelling each word with its grammatical role, such as noun or verb.
words.example: Part-of-speech tagging marks "run" as a verb in "I run daily".

words.definition: Finding names of people, places, organisations and similar items in text.
words.example: Named entity recognition tagged "Paris" as a location.

subjects.name: Computer Organization and Architecture
subjects.description: How the CPU, memory and digital logic actually run programs.

words.definition: The design of a computer as seen by the programmer, such as its instruction set.
words.example: x86 and ARM are different computer architectures.

words.definition: How the hardware parts are built and connected to implement the architecture.
words.example: Cache size is part of computer organization.

words.definition: A design where instructions and data share the same memory.
words.example: Most PCs follow the von Neumann architecture.

words.definition: The CPU: the part that fetches and executes instructions.
words.example: The central processing unit runs at 3 GHz.

words.definition: The ALU: the CPU part that does arithmetic and logic operations.
words.example: The arithmetic logic unit adds the two registers.

words.definition: The CPU part that decodes instructions and directs the other parts.
words.example: The control unit tells the ALU to subtract.

words.definition: A tiny, very fast storage location inside the CPU.
words.example: The sum is stored in register R1.

words.definition: The register holding the address of the next instruction.
words.example: A jump instruction changes the program counter.

words.definition: A single basic command the CPU can execute.
words.example: ADD R1, R2, R3 is one instruction.

words.definition: The full set of instructions, registers and rules a processor provides (ISA).
words.example: RISC-V is an open instruction set architecture.

words.definition: The part of an instruction that says which operation to perform.
words.example: In ADD R1, R2, R3 the opcode is ADD.

words.definition: A value or location an instruction works on.
words.example: R2 and R3 are the operands of the ADD.

words.definition: The rule for how an instruction finds its operand, such as immediate or register.
words.example: LOAD R1, #5 uses immediate addressing mode.

words.definition: Binary instructions the CPU executes directly.
words.example: The compiler turns C++ into machine code.

words.definition: A human-readable form of machine code, with one mnemonic per instruction.
words.example: MOV and ADD are assembly language mnemonics.

words.definition: A program that translates assembly language into machine code.
words.example: The assembler produced an object file.

words.definition: The repeated steps a CPU takes for each instruction: fetch it, decode it, execute it.
words.example: The fetch-decode-execute cycle runs billions of times a second.

words.definition: One tick of the CPU clock; the basic unit of time for hardware steps.
words.example: A 2 GHz clock has 2 billion clock cycles per second.

words.definition: The number of clock cycles per second, measured in hertz.
words.example: A higher clock rate alone doesn't guarantee a faster program.

words.definition: Cycles per instruction: the average number of clock cycles each instruction takes.
words.example: Lowering CPI speeds up the program at the same clock rate.

words.definition: Overlapping the stages of several instructions, like an assembly line.
words.example: Pipelining lets a new instruction start every cycle.

words.definition: A situation that stops the next instruction in a pipeline from running in its planned cycle.
words.example: Using a result before it is written causes a data hazard.

words.definition: Guessing which way a branch will go so the pipeline doesn't have to wait.
words.example: Good branch prediction keeps loops fast.

words.definition: Reduced Instruction Set Computer: a design with few, simple, fixed-length instructions.
words.example: ARM processors are RISC designs.

words.definition: Complex Instruction Set Computer: a design with many, varied, sometimes multi-step instructions.
words.example: x86 is a CISC architecture.

words.definition: A set of shared wires that carries data, addresses or control signals between parts.
words.example: The data bus carries 64 bits at a time.

words.definition: Layers of storage from small and fast (registers) to large and slow (disk).
words.example: Cache sits between registers and RAM in the memory hierarchy.

words.definition: Small, fast memory that keeps copies of recently used data near the CPU.
words.example: The L1 cache is the fastest level.

words.definition: When the requested data is found in the cache.
words.example: A cache hit takes only a few cycles.

words.definition: When the requested data is not in the cache and must be fetched from slower memory.
words.example: Each cache miss costs many cycles.

words.definition: The tendency of programs to reuse recent data (temporal) and nearby data (spatial).
words.example: Looping through an array in order uses spatial locality.

words.definition: The computer's RAM, which holds running programs and their data.
words.example: The program is loaded into main memory before it runs.

words.definition: Random Access Memory: fast, volatile memory that loses its contents without power.
words.example: The laptop has 16 GB of RAM.

words.definition: Read-Only Memory: non-volatile memory that keeps data without power, often holding firmware.
words.example: The startup firmware is stored in ROM.

words.definition: A technique that gives each program its own large address space, backed by RAM and disk.
words.example: Virtual memory lets programs use more memory than physically installed.

words.definition: A fixed-size block of virtual memory, often 4 KB.
words.example: The operating system moves a page from disk into RAM.

words.definition: A number identifying a location in memory.
words.example: Address 0x1000 holds the first instruction.

words.definition: The natural unit of data a processor handles at once.
words.example: A 64-bit CPU has a 64-bit word.

words.definition: The order in which the bytes of a multi-byte value are stored in memory.
words.example: x86 stores numbers in little-endian order; that is its endianness.

words.definition: The base-16 number system using digits 0-9 and A-F.
words.example: 255 is FF in hexadecimal.

words.definition: The usual way to store signed integers: invert the bits and add one to negate.
words.example: In 8-bit two's complement, -1 is 11111111.

words.definition: Storing real numbers as a sign, exponent and fraction, as in IEEE 754.
words.example: 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in floating-point representation.

words.definition: When a result is too large to fit in the available bits.
words.example: Adding 1 to 127 in 8-bit signed arithmetic causes overflow.

words.definition: A basic circuit that computes a Boolean function such as AND, OR or NOT.
words.example: A NAND logic gate can build any other gate.

words.definition: A table listing a circuit's output for every combination of inputs.
words.example: The truth table of XOR has outputs 0, 1, 1, 0.

words.definition: A circuit whose output depends only on its current inputs.
words.example: An adder is a combinational circuit.

words.definition: A circuit whose output depends on current inputs and stored past state.
words.example: A counter is a sequential circuit.

words.definition: A circuit that selects one of several inputs to pass to the output.
words.example: A 4-to-1 multiplexer uses 2 select lines.

words.definition: A circuit that adds binary numbers.
words.example: A full adder adds two bits plus a carry.

words.definition: A circuit that stores one bit and changes only on a clock edge.
words.example: A register is built from flip-flops.

words.definition: A signal that makes the CPU pause its current work to handle an event.
words.example: Pressing a key triggers an interrupt.

words.definition: Communication between the computer and outside devices (I/O).
words.example: Reading from a USB drive is input/output.

words.definition: DMA: devices transferring data to memory without the CPU copying each byte.
words.example: Direct memory access frees the CPU during disk reads.

words.definition: How much work is completed per unit of time.
words.example: Pipelining increases throughput.

words.definition: The delay between starting an operation and getting its result.
words.example: Memory latency is much higher than register latency.

words.definition: A chip with several independent CPU cores that can run tasks in parallel.
words.example: A quad-core multicore processor can run four threads at once.

subjects.name: SQL and Data Modelling
subjects.description: Writing SQL queries and designing data models.

words.definition: Structured Query Language, used to define, query and change relational data.
words.example: We wrote SQL to find the top students.

words.definition: Data Definition Language: SQL commands that define structure, such as CREATE and ALTER.
words.example: CREATE TABLE is a DDL command.

words.definition: Data Manipulation Language: SQL commands that change data, such as INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
words.example: UPDATE is a DML command.

words.definition: The SQL clause that chooses which columns to return.
words.example: SELECT name, email FROM Students;

words.definition: The SQL clause that names the table(s) a query reads data out of.
words.example: FROM Students tells the query where to look.

words.definition: The SQL clause that filters rows by a condition.
words.example: WHERE gpa > 3.5 keeps only top students.

words.definition: The SQL clause that sorts the results.
words.example: ORDER BY gpa DESC lists the highest first.

words.definition: The SQL clause that groups rows with the same values so aggregates can be computed per group.
words.example: GROUP BY major counts students in each major.

words.definition: The SQL clause that filters groups after GROUP BY.
words.example: HAVING COUNT(*) > 30 keeps only large majors.

words.definition: A function that computes one value from many rows, such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX.
words.example: AVG(gpa) is an aggregate function.

words.definition: A keyword that removes duplicate rows from the result.
words.example: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM Students;

words.definition: A temporary name for a column or table in a query, given with AS.
words.example: SELECT AVG(gpa) AS average_gpa uses an alias.

words.definition: An operator that matches text against a pattern with % and _.
words.example: WHERE name LIKE 'A%' finds names starting with A.

words.definition: An operator testing whether a value lies in an inclusive range.
words.example: WHERE age BETWEEN 18 AND 21.

words.definition: An operator testing whether a value matches any item of a list or subquery result.
words.example: WHERE major IN ('CS', 'Math').

words.definition: The test for a missing value; = NULL does not work.
words.example: WHERE phone IS NULL finds students without a phone.

words.definition: A clause that caps how many rows are returned (in MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQLite).
words.example: ORDER BY gpa DESC LIMIT 5 gives the top five.

words.definition: The SQL command that adds new rows.
words.example: INSERT INTO Students VALUES (1, 'Lola');

words.definition: The SQL command that changes existing rows.
words.example: UPDATE Students SET gpa = 3.8 WHERE id = 1;

words.definition: The SQL command that removes rows.
words.example: DELETE FROM Students WHERE id = 1;

words.definition: The SQL command that defines a new table.
words.example: CREATE TABLE Words (id INT PRIMARY KEY, text VARCHAR(50));

words.definition: The SQL command that changes a table's structure.
words.example: ALTER TABLE Words ADD level CHAR(2);

words.definition: The SQL command that deletes a table and all its data.
words.example: DROP TABLE Temp; removes the table completely.

words.definition: A text data type with a maximum length.
words.example: name VARCHAR(100) holds up to 100 characters.

words.definition: Combining rows from two tables based on a related column.
words.example: JOIN Enrolments ON Students.id = Enrolments.student_id.

words.definition: A join that returns only rows with a match in both tables.
words.example: INNER JOIN shows only students who are enrolled in something.

words.definition: A join that returns all rows from the left table, with NULLs where there is no match.
words.example: LEFT JOIN also shows students with no enrolments.

words.definition: A join that returns all rows from both tables, matching where possible.
words.example: FULL OUTER JOIN shows unmatched rows from both sides.

words.definition: Joining a table to itself.
words.example: A self join pairs each employee with their manager.

words.definition: A query nested inside another query.
words.example: WHERE gpa > (SELECT AVG(gpa) FROM Students) uses a subquery.

words.definition: A stored query that can be used like a table.
words.example: CREATE VIEW TopStudents AS SELECT ... WHERE gpa > 3.5;

words.definition: A structure that speeds up searches on a column.
words.example: CREATE INDEX idx_email ON Students(email);

words.definition: A rule on a column or table that the database enforces.
words.example: CHECK (gpa BETWEEN 0 AND 4) is a constraint.

words.definition: A constraint requiring a column to always have a value.
words.example: name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL.

words.definition: A constraint that stops two rows having the same value in a column.
words.example: email VARCHAR(100) UNIQUE.

words.definition: A constraint that requires each row to satisfy a condition.
words.example: CHECK (age >= 16).

words.definition: A value used for a column when no value is given.
words.example: created_at DATE DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE.

words.definition: The column(s) that uniquely identify each row; unique and not null.
words.example: id INT PRIMARY KEY.

words.definition: A column that references the primary key of another table.
words.example: FOREIGN KEY (student_id) REFERENCES Students(id).

words.definition: An artificial key, such as an auto-increment number or UUID, with no real-world meaning.
words.example: Each word has a UUID as a surrogate key.

words.definition: A key made from real-world data, such as a passport number or ISBN.
words.example: ISBN is a natural key for books.

words.definition: A description of how data is structured and related.
words.example: The data model shows Words, Topics and Users.

words.definition: A high-level data model of the main entities and relationships, without technical detail.
words.example: The conceptual model says a Student enrols in Courses.

words.definition: A data model with tables, columns and keys, independent of a specific DBMS.
words.example: The logical model adds keys to each entity.

words.definition: A data model with exact types, indexes and storage for a specific DBMS.
words.example: The physical model uses VARCHAR(100) for email in PostgreSQL.

words.definition: A thing about which data is stored, such as Student or Course.
words.example: Word is an entity in our data model.

words.definition: A property of an entity, which becomes a column.
words.example: level is an attribute of Word.

words.definition: An association between entities.
words.example: "Student enrols in Course" is a relationship.

words.definition: An ERD: a diagram of entities, attributes and relationships.
words.example: The entity-relationship diagram shows a many-to-many link.

words.definition: How many instances of one entity can relate to another: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many.
words.example: The cardinality of Teacher to Course is one-to-many.

words.definition: Describes a relationship where one row links to many rows in another table.
words.example: One teacher teaches many courses: one-to-many.

words.definition: Describes a relationship where many rows on each side link to many on the other.
words.example: Students and courses are many-to-many.

words.definition: A table that resolves a many-to-many relationship using two foreign keys.
words.example: Enrolments is the junction table between Students and Courses.

words.definition: Splitting tables to remove redundancy and update anomalies.
words.example: Normalization moved teacher details into their own table.

words.definition: Adding controlled redundancy to speed up reads.
words.example: Storing the word count on each topic is denormalization.

words.definition: A group of SQL statements that succeed or fail together.
words.example: BEGIN; ... COMMIT; wraps a transaction.

subjects.name: Theory of Automata
subjects.description: Abstract machines, formal languages and the limits of computation.

words.definition: A finite set of symbols, written Σ.
words.example: Σ = {0, 1} is the binary alphabet.

words.definition: A finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet.
words.example: 0110 is a string over {0, 1}.

words.definition: The string with no symbols, written ε or λ.
words.example: The empty string has length 0.

words.definition: A set of strings over an alphabet.
words.example: All binary strings ending in 0 form a formal language.

words.definition: Joining two strings or languages end to end.
words.example: The concatenation of ab and ba is abba.

words.definition: The operation L* giving all concatenations of zero or more strings from L.
words.example: {a}* = {ε, a, aa, aaa, ...} by the Kleene star.

words.definition: An abstract machine that reads input and changes state according to rules (plural: automata).
words.example: A vending machine can be modelled as an automaton.

words.definition: One of the configurations an automaton can be in.
words.example: The machine moves to state q1 after reading a 1.

words.definition: The state where an automaton begins.
words.example: q0 is the start state.

words.definition: A state that means the input is accepted if the machine ends there; also called a final state.
words.example: The string is accepted because it ends in an accept state.

words.definition: A move from one state to another on reading a symbol.
words.example: There is a transition from q0 to q1 on input a.

words.definition: The function δ giving the next state(s) for each state and input symbol.
words.example: δ(q0, 1) = q1 is part of the transition function.

words.definition: A drawing of an automaton with circles for states and arrows for transitions.
words.example: The state diagram has a double circle for the accept state.

words.definition: An automaton with a finite number of states and no extra memory.
words.example: A finite automaton can check if a binary number is even.

words.definition: A DFA: each state has exactly one transition for each input symbol.
words.example: A deterministic finite automaton never has to guess.

words.definition: An NFA: a state may have zero, one or several transitions on a symbol, or ε-moves.
words.example: A nondeterministic finite automaton accepts if any path ends in an accept state.

words.definition: Allowing a machine several possible next moves at once.
words.example: Nondeterminism makes some automata much smaller to draw.

words.definition: A move that changes state without reading any input.
words.example: The NFA uses an epsilon transition to skip the optional sign.

words.definition: The method that converts an NFA into an equivalent DFA whose states are sets of NFA states.
words.example: Subset construction can create up to 2^n DFA states.

words.definition: Producing the DFA with the fewest states that accepts the same language.
words.example: DFA minimization merged three equivalent states.

words.definition: A pattern describing a regular language using union, concatenation and star.
words.example: (0|1)*0 is a regular expression for binary strings ending in 0.

words.definition: A language recognised by some finite automaton, or described by a regular expression.
words.example: Valid identifiers in C++ form a regular language.

words.definition: A fact that applying an operation to languages of a class gives a language in the same class.
words.example: Regular languages have the closure property under union.

words.definition: A property all regular (or context-free) languages have, used to prove a language is not in that class.
words.example: The pumping lemma shows {a^n b^n} is not regular.

words.definition: A theorem that a language is regular exactly when it has finitely many distinguishable classes of prefixes.
words.example: The Myhill-Nerode theorem also explains DFA minimization.

words.definition: A set of rules for generating the strings of a language.
words.example: The grammar S → aSb | ε generates a^n b^n.

words.definition: A grammar where each rule replaces a single non-terminal.
words.example: Programming language syntax is usually given as a context-free grammar.

words.definition: A rule showing how a non-terminal can be replaced.
words.example: S → aSb is a production rule.

words.definition: A symbol that appears in the final strings and is not replaced.
words.example: In S → aSb, a and b are terminals.

words.definition: A variable symbol in a grammar that gets replaced by rules.
words.example: S is a non-terminal.

words.definition: The non-terminal that every derivation begins from.
words.example: S is the start symbol of the grammar.

words.definition: A sequence of rule applications producing a string from the start symbol.
words.example: S ⇒ aSb ⇒ ab is a derivation.

words.definition: A tree showing how a string is derived from a grammar.
words.example: The parse tree shows that * is applied before +.

words.definition: A grammar where some string has more than one parse tree.
words.example: E → E + E | E * E | id is an ambiguous grammar.

words.definition: A language generated by a context-free grammar.
words.example: {a^n b^n} is a context-free language.

words.definition: A grammar form where every rule is A → BC or A → a (plus S → ε if needed).
words.example: The CYK algorithm needs the grammar in Chomsky normal form.

words.definition: A finite automaton plus a stack; it recognises context-free languages.
words.example: A pushdown automaton checks balanced brackets.

words.definition: The last-in, first-out memory of a pushdown automaton.
words.example: The PDA pushes an a onto the stack for each a it reads.

words.definition: An abstract machine with a finite control and an infinite tape it can read and write; the standard model of computation.
words.example: A Turing machine can simulate any algorithm.

words.definition: The unbounded sequence of cells a Turing machine reads and writes.
words.example: The input starts on the tape.

words.definition: The part of a Turing machine that reads and writes one cell and moves left or right.
words.example: The tape head moves right after writing X.

words.definition: The claim that anything computable by an algorithm can be computed by a Turing machine.
words.example: By the Church-Turing thesis, C++ can't solve problems a Turing machine can't.

words.definition: Describes a problem for which some algorithm always halts with the correct yes/no answer.
words.example: Checking whether a DFA accepts a string is decidable.

words.definition: Describes a problem that no algorithm can solve for every input.
words.example: The halting problem is undecidable.

words.definition: Describes a language for which a Turing machine accepts every member, though it may run forever on non-members.
words.example: The halting problem is recognizable but not decidable.

words.definition: The problem of deciding whether a given program halts on a given input.
words.example: Turing proved the halting problem cannot be solved in general.

words.definition: Turning one problem into another, to show the second is at least as hard.
words.example: A reduction from the halting problem proves a new problem undecidable.

words.definition: The classification of languages into regular, context-free, context-sensitive and recursively enumerable.
words.example: Regular languages are the lowest level of the Chomsky hierarchy.

words.definition: A finite-state machine whose output depends on the current state and input.
words.example: A Mealy machine outputs a symbol on each transition.

words.definition: A finite-state machine whose output depends only on the current state.
words.example: A traffic light controller is a Moore machine.

words.definition: A set of problems that can be solved within a given resource limit, such as time.
words.example: P and NP are complexity classes.

words.definition: The class of decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic machine.
words.example: Sorting-based problems like checking for duplicates are in P.

words.definition: The class of decision problems whose yes-answers can be checked in polynomial time.
words.example: Sudoku solutions are easy to check, so the problem is in NP.

words.definition: Describes the hardest problems in NP; if one is solvable in polynomial time, all of NP is.
words.example: SAT was the first problem proved NP-complete.
